q: Bahans Haut-Brion disappeared from wine lists after the 2006 vintage, although the wine behind the name did not. What is that second wine called now?
accept: le clarence de haut brion the second wine
exp: The name honours Clarence Dillon, the American financier who bought the property in 1935, and the change lined the second wine up with the family name used across the group. Second labels are renamed often enough that a wine list can be years out of date without anyone noticing, which is reason enough to check the vintage against the name.

q: One Ribera del Duero bodega sells a red in its fifth year, drawn from the same vineyards as a flagship it holds back roughly twice as long. Name the wine released early.
exp: The number in its name counts the years from harvest to release rather than anything about the blend, and the fruit comes off the same estate rather than off lesser ground. Selling a serious wine early is a cash decision as much as a stylistic one, since a cellar holding stock for a decade has to be paid for somehow.

q: A Napa estate founded as a Franco-American partnership sells a second wine blended across several harvests, so it carries no vintage at all. Name it.
exp: Blending several years into one red is ordinary in Champagne and rare in Napa, where the vintage date is treated as part of the claim. It is sold largely at the winery rather than through the trade, which is why it turns up on wine lists far less often than the estate's flagship does.

q: Printed on a French label the word Chateau is not decoration, and it may be used only where a pair of conditions are met. Which pair?
opts: The grapes all come off the estate's own vines, and the wine is vinified there
The estate holds a rank in a recognised classification, and a building stands on the land
The fruit is grown and bottled in the same commune, and the label states the year the estate was founded
The property sits inside a communal appellation, and its owner farms at least ten hectares
exp: The rule is about the fruit and the winemaking rather than about architecture: every grape must be grown on the named holding and the wine made there, so plenty of chateaux are sheds and plenty of grand houses have no vines at all. It comes from the same body of French law that governs Domaine, Clos, Cru and Abbaye, all of them traditional terms with conditions attached rather than free adjectives.

q: In Jerez a private stockholder buys young wine, ages a few butts of it in a warehouse of his own and sells the result on to the shippers rather than bottling under his own name. What is he called?
exp: The word means warehouseman, and the trade grew up because ageing stock is slow money that a small holder can afford to tie up and a shipper would rather buy than carry. Some of those soleras are now bottled under the almacenista's name alongside the shipper's, which is how a category that existed to be invisible became collectable.

q: Until 1986 no Port could be exported unless it had first been aged in one town across the river from Oporto, which is why the quintas up the valley shipped nothing under their own names. Name that town.
accept: vila nova de gaia across the douro
exp: The rule bound the trade to the shippers' lodges and to their entrepot, so a grower who wanted to sell abroad had to sell to a shipper first. Its repeal is why estates up the valley began bottling and exporting under their own names from the late 1980s, and the modern shape of the Douro trade follows from it.

q: A Burgundian grower who buys grapes as well as farming his own registers a second business for the bought fruit, and by long convention its bottles open with a different word from the estate's. Which word?
exp: Domaine is reserved by law for wine off the grower's own vines and Maison signals a merchant business, even where one family runs both from one cellar. Maison is defined nowhere at all, which is why a house that farms not a single row may call itself one with nobody's permission; what the law polices is the word Domaine, and the merchant word is left to the trade's own convention.

q: Barrels sold at the Hospices de Beaune auction are catalogued under cuvee names that appear on no map of the slope, and the buyer's own cellar raises and bottles the wine afterwards. What do those cuvee names record?
accept: the benefactors who gave the vineyards
the people who donated the vines
the people who gave the vineyards to the hospices
the donors who left vines to the hospital
ans: The benefactors who gave the vineyards
exp: The hospital has been left vines since the fifteenth century, and each bequest is kept as a named cuvee rather than folded into the rest, so the catalogue reads as a list of benefactors. A cuvee may draw on parcels in more than one climat, which is exactly why those names cannot be found on any vineyard map.

q: Long before grafting, a grower who lost a vine bent a cane down from the plant beside it, buried the middle of that cane until it took root and then cut it free. Which operation is this?
exp: The new plant grows on its own roots and carries the parent's material exactly, so a plot renewed this way keeps whatever selection was originally in it. It also explains why old ungrafted parcels are irregularly spaced: a vine put there by layering stands where its parent could reach, not where a surveyor wanted it.

q: Small walled parcels at Ay carry Pinot Noir that was never grafted onto American rootstock, and the blanc de noirs made from them runs to a few thousand bottles in the years it appears. Name that cuvee.
exp: French old vines is all the name claims, and the point of it is the ungrafted stock rather than the age of any particular plant. A third parcel at Bouzy was lost to phylloxera and grubbed up in the 2000s, which is a reminder that such plots survive by constant work rather than by luck.

q: A single Yountville vineyard planted in the nineteenth century supplies the whole of a Napa red whose name is the Latin for lord and master of the house. Name the vineyard.
exp: Napanook was among the first vineyards planted in that part of the valley and its fruit was sold to other wineries for most of a century before it was bottled on its own. Yountville sits between the cool of Oak Knoll and the warmth of Oakville, which is much of why the wine is built on structure rather than on ripeness.

q: A Bordeaux family that had already founded a Napa joint venture set up a second one in the 1990s on Andean gravels in the upper Maipo, and the wine took its name from a character in Beaumarchais. Name it.
exp: Count Almaviva belongs to The Marriage of Figaro, and the label carries a design borrowed from Mapuche art, so the bottle advertises both partners at once. The Chilean partner was already growing Cabernet of the first rank on that stretch of gravel, which is why the ground was settled before the deal was.

q: A Saint-Emilion first growth and a Mendoza estate share a Malbec-led red grown on stony Andean ground at around a thousand metres. Name that wine.
accept: the cheval des andes joint venture
exp: Malbec leads it and Cabernet Sauvignon fills it out, which is the Bordeaux partner's contribution to a grape Argentina had long bottled on its own. Mendoza's old ungrafted Malbec is the material such ventures are really after, since cuttings of that quality no longer exist in the variety's homeland.

q: Mosel estates have always aged in a large oval cask of about a thousand litres, and older price lists quote a crop by the number of them filled. Name that cask.
exp: A thousand litres of wine touching that much oak takes almost nothing from the wood, which is exactly the point on a Riesling meant to taste of slate and fruit. The half-size cask is a Halbfuder and the Rhine's equivalent is larger again, and all of them are giving way in many cellars to steel, which does the same job of adding nothing at all.

q: Bordeaux quotes a crop and a price in a unit that no cellar actually contains: nine hundred litres, or four barriques. Name that unit.
exp: Nine hundred litres is twelve hundred bottles, or a hundred cases of twelve, so a chateau's crop and an opening price are both still discussed in tonneaux although the wine never sits in one. It is a unit of account inherited from the days when claret travelled in cask, and it survives because everyone in the trade can convert it in their head.

q: Northern Rhone cellars often raise Syrah in a cask of about six hundred litres, larger than a barrique and smaller than a foudre, chosen so that the oak marks the wine less. Name it.
exp: Half a muid, the muid being an old measure that varied from town to town, so the name is a fossil of a unit nobody uses any more. The wider stave and the lower ratio of wood to wine give slower oxygen and much less vanilla than a barrique, which is why estates trying to lighten their oak move to this size rather than merely to older barrels.
